blocks.text: Matthew 4 moves from Jesus’ wilderness testing to the beginning of his public work in Galilee. Across these scenes, Matthew connects Jesus’ sonship with Scripture, presents repentance as the response to the approaching kingdom of heaven, and summarizes Jesus’ ministry as teaching, proclaiming, healing, and driving out demons.

During most of Jesus’ ministry, Galilee was governed by Herod Antipas rather than by the Roman prefect of Judea. Its villages supported farming, fishing, crafts, and local markets, with travel occurring along both lake and land routes. This setting gives concrete social and economic shape to Jesus’ movement through Galilee and to his encounter with working fishermen beside the sea.

Capernaum was a lake-side settlement of basalt-built domestic compounds near regional routes. It belonged to the Roman-period Galilean lake economy, so Jesus’ move there places his activity within a village environment connected to fishing, households, and regional movement. Archaeology clarifies this settlement setting, but it cannot identify particular excavated rooms with specific Gospel events.

sections.title: Village Life and the Fishermen’s Calling

blocks.text: Early Roman Galilee was substantially Jewish while still displaying local variation and participating in wider regional exchange. Village and household life, synagogue gatherings, purity practices, festivals, and subsistence work all formed part of this setting. Galilee therefore should not be imagined either as detached from Jewish life or as simply identical to Jerusalem and its institutions.

The calling of Simon Peter, Andrew, James, and John occurs within a social world shaped by family networks, kinship obligations, vocation, household economy, travel, and public reputation. Matthew makes several of these features visible: the men work as fishermen, James and John share a boat with their father, and both pairs are occupied with the tools of their livelihood when Jesus calls them.

Scripture shapes the presentation of Jesus at two important points. In the wilderness, Jesus answers each temptation with Scripture, particularly words from Deuteronomy, while the devil also quotes Scripture in the second test. Later, Matthew introduces the words of Isaiah with a fulfillment formula to interpret Jesus’ move into Galilee. Matthew’s scriptural citations may draw on varied Hebrew and Greek forms, making Scripture part of the narrative’s explanation rather than merely an added ornament.

Jesus’ public proclamation begins with repentance because the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. Matthew then depicts this proclamation alongside teaching, healing, and exorcism. Readers may differ over how these activities relate in detail, but Matthew’s summary deliberately places the announcement of the kingdom beside actions addressing disease, bodily affliction, and conditions understood in terms of hostile spirits.

sections.title: How the Chapter’s Parts Work Together

blocks.text: The chapter’s major movements illuminate one another. The wilderness testing presents Jesus’ sonship through a contest over faithful use of Scripture; the Isaiah citation interprets the beginning of his Galilean work; the kingdom announcement states the message of that work; and the closing summary shows it taking visible form through teaching, proclamation, healing, and exorcism. Reading these features together helps explain why Matthew presents Jesus’ words, movements, and actions as parts of one opening portrait of his ministry.
